questions.q: A Malaysian court barred Christians from using the word “Allah.” How does the editorial suggest Malaysian Muslims should see the matter?
options: As an insult that calls for protest
Not quite. The article says: As common ground and a starting point for dialogue about the oneness of God.
As proof that the two faiths cannot live together
Not quite. The article says: As common ground and a starting point for dialogue about the oneness of God.
As a legal matter best left to the courts
Not quite. The article says: As common ground and a starting point for dialogue about the oneness of God.
As common ground and a starting point for dialogue about the oneness of God
Yes. The Quran invites to “a word common to us.”
questions.rationale: “Historically, the word ‘Allah’ has never been the monopoly of Muslims… Malaysian Muslims should welcome it and avail it as an opportunity for spiritual exchange.”

questions.article: Dua, According to the Quran and the Bible
questions.q: Why does the article call dua (supplication) “the essence of worship”?
options: It can replace all other duties
Not quite. The article says: It springs from realising that God is the Giver and man wholly dependent on Him.
It must be said in a fixed form of words
Not quite. The article says: It springs from realising that God is the Giver and man wholly dependent on Him.
It is the easiest act of worship to perform
Not quite. The article says: It springs from realising that God is the Giver and man wholly dependent on Him.
It springs from realising that God is the Giver and man wholly dependent on Him
Right. That realisation turns a person to God at once.
questions.rationale: “When Man discovers God through his absolute attributes, he also discovers that, in comparison to God, he has no significance at all… it makes him immediately turn to God in supplication.”

questions.q: The article describes how, over generations, a prophet’s community changes its idea of salvation. What is the change?
options: Rituals grow fewer and simpler
Not quite. The article says: Good tidings given for faith and deeds come to be claimed as the birthright of the group.
The community forgets its prophet’s name
Not quite. The article says: Good tidings given for faith and deeds come to be claimed as the birthright of the group.
Good tidings given for faith and deeds come to be claimed as the birthright of the group
Exactly. Religion turns into “a kind of national heritage.”
People stop believing in the Hereafter
Not quite. The article says: Good tidings given for faith and deeds come to be claimed as the birthright of the group.
questions.rationale: “Tidings which had been given on the basis of faith and righteous actions come to be considered to be the result of ethnic affiliations… But God does not have a special relationship with any particular community.”

questions.q: What happens, according to the article, in a society that takes away freedom of expression?
options: People turn to science instead of opinion
Not quite. The article says: People go on thinking but hide their thoughts, so it fills with hypocrites and stagnates.
People become more religious
Not quite. The article says: People go on thinking but hide their thoughts, so it fills with hypocrites and stagnates.
People go on thinking but hide their thoughts, so it fills with hypocrites and stagnates
Yes. Sincerity and creativity both need freedom.
People stop thinking and live in harmony
Not quite. The article says: People go on thinking but hide their thoughts, so it fills with hypocrites and stagnates.
questions.rationale: “If people are deprived of the right to free expression, it will not stop them from thinking, but it will certainly stop them from expressing their thoughts… [it] will finally be full of hypocrites.”

questions.q: Sir James Jeans wrote that man seems to have “strayed into a world that was not made for him.” How does the article explain this feeling?
options: Man has damaged the earth beyond repair
Not quite. The article says: Man’s nature seeks complete fulfilment, which this limited world cannot give; his true home is Paradise.
Man came to earth from another planet
Not quite. The article says: Man’s nature seeks complete fulfilment, which this limited world cannot give; his true home is Paradise.
Man’s nature seeks complete fulfilment, which this limited world cannot give; his true home is Paradise
Well reasoned. The earth is a selection ground.
Man’s desires are a sickness to be cured
Not quite. The article says: Man’s nature seeks complete fulfilment, which this limited world cannot give; his true home is Paradise.
questions.rationale: “There is a contradiction between man’s nature, which seeks fulfilment of his desires, and the world, which is incapable of fulfilling man’s desires… Man’s eternal habitat lies in the world Hereafter.”

questions.q: The Makkan envoys asked King Negus to hand over the Muslim migrants without questioning them. What did he do?
options: He refused to decide until he had heard the migrants himself
Yes. Justice means hearing both sides.
He accepted the gifts and sent the migrants back
Not quite. The article says: He refused to decide until he had heard the migrants himself.
He expelled both groups from his land
Not quite. The article says: He refused to decide until he had heard the migrants himself.
He asked his courtiers to decide
Not quite. The article says: He refused to decide until he had heard the migrants himself.
questions.rationale: Negus said: “I will never hand them over to you, unless they are called before me and I speak to them.” The article says judging on one side’s account is “a form of oppression.”

questions.q: Which of these did NOT sway Negus in reaching his decision?
options: Only his courtiers; the gifts pleased him
Not quite. The article says: All of them left him unmoved – gifts, his courtiers’ advice and the migrants’ differing belief about Jesus.
All of them left him unmoved – gifts, his courtiers’ advice and the migrants’ differing belief about Jesus
Correct. He “focused only on the issue of justice.”
Only the gifts; the courtiers persuaded him
Not quite. The article says: All of them left him unmoved – gifts, his courtiers’ advice and the migrants’ differing belief about Jesus.
Only the difference of belief; he took offence
Not quite. The article says: All of them left him unmoved – gifts, his courtiers’ advice and the migrants’ differing belief about Jesus.
questions.rationale: “Negus was not influenced by the gifts of the Makkan delegation. Nor did he accept the advice and recommendations of his courtiers… The King did not bother about all this.”

questions.q: The article uses the electric light switch as an example. What is it meant to teach?
options: Electricity should be used sparingly
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude has to be discovered by reflection; one who does not acknowledge people will not acknowledge God.
Modern inventions distract us from God
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude has to be discovered by reflection; one who does not acknowledge people will not acknowledge God.
Scientists deserve more thanks than anyone
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude has to be discovered by reflection; one who does not acknowledge people will not acknowledge God.
Gratitude has to be discovered by reflection; one who does not acknowledge people will not acknowledge God
Right. We take blessings for granted.
questions.rationale: “Shukr is not a ready-made thing. We have to apply our intellect to discover it… when they fail to acknowledge man, they also fail to acknowledge God.”

questions.q: After the date-palm growers of Medina had a poor crop, the Prophet told them, “You know the matters of the world better than I do.” What principle does the article draw?
options: Matters governed by the laws of nature belong to observation and experiment, not to religious ruling
Exactly. This separation opened the door to science.
Tradition is always wiser than new ideas
Not quite. The article says: Matters governed by the laws of nature belong to observation and experiment, not to religious ruling.
Prophets should not speak on daily life
Not quite. The article says: Matters governed by the laws of nature belong to observation and experiment, not to religious ruling.
Farmers need not follow religion
Not quite. The article says: Matters governed by the laws of nature belong to observation and experiment, not to religious ruling.
questions.rationale: “What is demonstrable in nature, yielding itself to research and experiment, will be accepted by Islam as established, empirical knowledge.”

questions.q: Why, in the author’s view, do interfaith conferences achieve so little?
options: They treat a social question – how people of different faiths live together – as a theological one
Yes. The answer is peaceful coexistence, not unity of religions.
They exclude ordinary believers
Not quite. The article says: They treat a social question – how people of different faiths live together – as a theological one.
They are opposed by governments
Not quite. The article says: They treat a social question – how people of different faiths live together – as a theological one.
They are held too rarely
Not quite. The article says: They treat a social question – how people of different faiths live together – as a theological one.
questions.rationale: “The problem is basically social, rather than theological… the ‘unity of faiths’ and ‘social unity of people of different faiths’ are two different and distinct issues.”
